utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that there are no preliminaries. But before we start, Judge Fluegge is for urgent personal reasons unable to sit today. We expect him back tomorrow. Judge Moloto and I have considered whether it would be in the interest of justice to continue to hear the case. We concluded that it is. Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Estimates for today are one hour in chief, Ms. MacGregor, and two hours for cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Wright, I presume.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Wright, before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Wright, when I am addressing you as "Mr. Wright" and not as "Professor Wright, it has got nothing to do with not fully appreciating your professional standards. It's a habit in this court that we call people by their rather than by rank or title.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. MacGregor will now examine you. Ms. MacGregor is counsel for the Prosecution. You'll find her to your right. Ms. MacGregor, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor Wright. If you can please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: My full name is Richard Vernon Stafford Wright.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And I remind you and also myself that we must pause between our questions and answers since we are both speaking in the same language to wait for the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If the court officer can please show 65 ter 29102. I believe this has been loaded into e-court. If not, please let me know. This is --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is not in e-court, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honours. Ms. Stewart informs me that it's being released just now. Would you like the 65 ter number again? Okay. Your Honours, this is an updated copy of Professor Wright's CV which is the reason for the new 65 ter number. I've provided a copy to the Defence. Unfortunately there is not yet a B/C/S translation, although there are very few differences with the prior copy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It takes a few minutes from the moment it's released until --

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Perhaps instead, then, we should show the older version and that is at 65 ter 05334. I can then question the witness about the significant differences that would have come up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed as you suggest.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Professor Wright, if you see on the screen in front of you there is a copy of the -- actually, I'm just checking. The one on the right is in English. Is this a copy of your CV?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And as you have heard, it is not the most recent version that you have provided but does it summarise for the most part your educational and professional background?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Now it lists you as an emeritus professor of anthropology, although the reports you have provided to the Tribunal are archeological in nature. Can you explain the difference?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, in the older universities the word "anthropology" covered human evolution and physical anthropology, that's bones. It covered archeology other than classical archeology, and it covered cultural anthropology. So I was an archeologist within a department of anthropology in the broad umbrella of the term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. MacGregor, I am informed that the uploading into e-court is complete by now. So perhaps we could work on the basis of the newest version.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And the 65 ter for that is 29102.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Professor Wright, when the new document comes on the screen, which it is now there, is this a copy of the more current version of the CV?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I'll have to see the end of the last page to see the date, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Are you able to see?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, I haven't updated it since then.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If the Registrar can turn back to the first page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: There is an AM listed beside your name that was not included on the prior copy of your CV. Can you explain what that means?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, that means I was made a Member of the Order of Australia for forensic work that I've done.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: When you say "the Order of Australia," what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: It's an honour granted by the Governor-General of Australia.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution tenders Professor Wright's CV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the absence of any objections, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 29102 receives number P1760, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Professor Wright, you have testified at the Tribunal several times as an expert about your work on exhumations for the Office of the Prosecution. Which cases have you testified in?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I testified in the case of Krstic, Tolimir, Popovic et al., and Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to review the statement that the Prosecution is tendering of yours today which is part of your Krstic and Karadzic testimony?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, I did review that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And was that testimony true to the best of your knowledge when you gave it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Would you give the same answers in substance if asked the same questions today?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution tenders the 92 ter statement for Professor Wright under 65 ter number -- I'm sorry, Ms. Stewart is telling me that there is not yet a 65 ter number. If you can give me one moment. Your Honours, it was tendered by the Prosecution in its Rule 92 ter motion submitted, which the Defence has responded to. However, due to my oversight, I did not include it on the exhibit list so it does not have a 65 ter number. The motion was filed by the Prosecution on July 1st, 2013. I don't know if there is a mechanism for directing the Chamber's attention to it now so that it can be seen. I know that the Defence has seen it and has replied to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've read it, but if there is no 65 ter number and if there is no exhibit number, then I'm afraid that we are unable to consult it on our screens. If Ms. Stewart would be in a position to show it in Sanction, then we could at least have it on our screens. I have the hard copy in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I'll -- as is, I think, probably, evident, the Prosecution will be tendering that statement. It is not a written statement with a signature, so I don't need to show it to the witness in order to have him recognise his signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But for admission we need to have it in the system, otherwise we restart a paper trial, which this is not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, would it be possible to continue with the examination while Ms. Stewart's colleague uploads it into e-court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at the Defence. Mr. Stojanovic, any problem? No problems. We'll continue as you suggest.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you. And thank you also to my colleagues for their efforts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Once it has been assigned a 65 ter number, then, of course, you should ask leave to add it to your 65 ter list. And after that, we can consider whether or not we'll -- once tendered, whether we can admit it or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Would it be wise to delay the reading of the witness's 92 ter summary into evidence until that point or should I go ahead and do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor Wright started work for the ICTY in 1997. In 1998 he led the exhumations at the mass grave sites at the Red Dam, Cancari Road 3, Cancari Road 12, Hodzici Road 3, 4, and 5, Liplje 2, and Zeleni Jadar 5. In 1999 he exhumed a primary mass grave at Kozluk and at Kevljani. In 2000 he led the exhumations at Glogova, Pasinac, and Redak. Professor Wright began his examinations when he would be taken by ICTY investigators to a suspected mass grave site. It was then his job to find the actual location of the grave within that suspect area. First the site was checked for mines and booby-traps and a surveying team was set up to record the grave's contents. A backhoe would then be used to scrape off the surface of the soil until Professor Wright was satisfied that the complete outline of the grave had been uncovered. Each of the bodies within the grave was surveyed with a three-dimensional recording system, and each body or body part was photographed and assigned a unique number. When a virtually complete body was removed, the experts also filled out a form called a "body sheet" which described the properties of the body. Once the bodies and body parts had been exhumed, they were sent to the morgue for anthropological and pathological analysis. Professor Wright would also examine and note any artefacts or other items contained in the graves, in addition to noting any significant factors related to the structure, composition, or nature of the graves. Professor Wright summarised his findings in written reports which he provided to the Office of the Prosecutor. May I now continue with questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Professor Wright, in the summary I just read, I referenced several reports that you wrote on exhumations. And as you know, the Prosecution is tendering those reports that you did on your exhumations in Prijedor and Srebrenica. Did you have an opportunity to review those reports before testifying today?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And do you still stand by the analysis and conclusions of those reports?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If the court officer can please show the 1998 report, which is 65 ter 04603, page 24 in e-court in the English version and page 26 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And, Professor Wright, in a few moments, a section from your report from 1998 will come on the screen. This is the section on Hodzici 04. To the right of your screen is the English version, and if you look at the section near the bottom H --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam MacGregor, is it 04 or 05?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, on the screen we see 05.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Now we do see 04 too.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If you can please direct your attention to section HZ04, the fourth paragraph in the section, it's actually the last sentence on the page, this sentence says: "Dr. Tony Brown visited the exhumation, and on the basis of several properties concludes that the graves at Lazete are the origin of HZ05." Now should this sentence be referring to grave HZ05 or HZ04?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I made a typological error there. It should refer to HZ04.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And if we can please look at the next paragraph. And the court officer, this will require turning to the next page in the English although staying on the same page in B/C/S. We'll give the document a moment to catch up.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If you see the first sentence on your page, and in B/C/S this is the last sentence in the section on HZ04, and this is essentially the same question. We see a reference to HZ05 and what should that actually be referring to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: It should refer to HZ04. It's the same mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And I will no longer need that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I want to move on now to discuss in general your methodology in conducting exhumations and in writing the reports for the Office of the Prosecution. How were you initially contacted to lead exhumations for the OTP?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I was contacted by the then deputy -- Deputy Prosecutor, Mr. Graham Blewitt, and asked if I would head up the team for '97 that was going to be working at Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Did you have prior experience or training with mass grave exhumations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, I did. In 1990 and 1991, I was employed by the Australian Attorney-General's Department to exhume three mass graves in the Ukraine. These dated from 1942 and were the subject of an investigation by the Australian Attorney-General into three men who were then Australians in 1990 but who were charged with war crimes in the Ukraine. And the Attorney-General's Department if there were these graves in the Ukraine that eye-witnesses were alleging, and so I exhumed three of those graves.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And approximately, and this doesn't need to be specific, but what amount of people or victims were in the mass graves?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: In the 1990 grave that we excavated at a place called Serniki, that's S-e-r-n-i-k-i, there were about 553, mainly women and children and old men. And in 1991, we didn't exhume the whole grave, we just exhumed at Ustinovska children who had been killed after the adults had been killed. But there were approximately 160 individuals there. And at a site called Gnivan, G-n-i-v-a-n, there were about 120.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. MacGregor, we're listening with great attention to what Mr. Wright tells us but we had read that already in the previous testimony, so therefore could we avoid repetition.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is not because we are not interested, Mr. Wright, but because we've read it already, you testified about it before. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Were you familiar with the professional backgrounds of your team members on the OTP exhumations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I was towards the end but not at the beginning. At the beginning I knew -- did not know enough people who could make up a team and Jose Pablo Baraybar suggested names to me of -- that were members -- to be members of the team. But by the year 2000, I knew the field, so to speak, and made up my own team.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Were you present at the excavations for the duration of them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, I was always present at the excavations unless I was sick or went on leave, in which case a deputy was appointed. But I was present in the grave, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And as the director or the lead of the excavations, what was your role while the excavation was happening?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: My main role was to see that the protocols that we'd established were being followed by the excavators and the surveyors and the photographers. In other words, I would be checking that things were working properly according to our protocols.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: When it came time to write the reports that you'd been contracted to write, what sources of your own did you review in order to write the reports?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Well, sources of my own were notebooks which have already been copied for ICTY, that is, personal notebooks, but the main information was contained within survey data, photographic data, and the excavation logs which contained sequentially each item that was discovered, whether it was a body or a body part or an artefact.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And did you consult any sources of others or reports of others to write your own reports?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, I was constantly in touch with Ian Hanson who was doing most of the surveying, Tim Loveless who did the photography, and the scenes of crime officers who compiled the logs.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this point I would like to offer into evidence -- there are four reports that relate to Srebrenica graves and there are three reports that relate to Prijedor graves. I can go through the seven 65 ter numbers when you're ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are ready.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Okay. The Kozluk report is 04602. Eastern Bosnia report, 04603. Glogova 1, 04611. Kevljani, 11049. Pasinac, 11051. Glogova Site 1, Grave L, 11052. And Redak 1, 11053.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I apologise, though, could you please repeat the report for the Redak grave, the 65 ter. If I understood it correctly, it's 11053.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It doesn't appear with that number on the transcript --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- but now it does. Madam Registrar, could you assign numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 04602 receives number P1761. Document 04603 receives number P1762. Document 04611 receives number P1763. Document 11049 receives number P1764. Document 11051 receives number P1765. Document 11052 receives number P1766. And document 11053 receives number P1767, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1761 up to and including P1767 are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Also, Ms. Stewart has just informed me that the 92 ter excerpts that -- excuse me, the transcript excerpts that comprise Professor Wright's statement are now uploaded. If I can provide those, would this be a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: The 65 ter numbers are 21903 and 29104. I was going to, again, tender those into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it after you have sought leave to add them to your 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections? Mr. Stojanovic remains silent, therefore I take it that he has no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 29103 receives number P1768, Your Honours. And document 29104 receives number P1769, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1768 and P1769 are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I can ask the court officer to show Exhibit 1762.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Professor Wright, while that's loading I've asked the court officer to show your 1998 report on exhumations in Eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If we can please look at page 172 in e-court in the English version. This is a photograph and I've discovered that the B/C/S version did not include the photos, which means the captions to this photograph does not have a translation. So that is something we can address at a later time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I've asked the court officer to show a photo that relates to the Cancari Road 12 grave. Are you able to see that photo on the screen in front of you Professor Wright?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I can see the top part of it, not the whole.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Okay. If we need to, I'll ask the court officer to zoom out. Now you have stated that you customarily removed bodies as you excavated, sort of as you went. If we look at this photo, it appears that there is a mass of remains in place. Can you explain why you left the bodies in place for this particular excavation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. We wanted to get an idea of the distribution of bodies within the grave, and since the weather conditions were reasonable and we could cover the bodies at night, we decided to display the top layer of bodies within the grave. There are many more underneath that are not showing. But that was at a measure that we took at Cancari 12, but in general, with the exception of one area of the Kozluk site, we removed the bodies as we found them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: On the left of that photograph we see a trench. Can you just explain for the Chamber what that is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: That trench allows us to see the bodies from the side, the layers of bodies from the side, and it also serves to drain the area. If it should rain, we don't want water rising and disturbing the bodies and the evidence, so we pump water out of that trench.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: So to be clear, that's a trench that was put there by the excavation team?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: By us, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And this will help with the captions which have not been translated, can you just very briefly explain the significance that is described in the caption in the second sentence about the spilling over on the right side of where the bodies are?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. In the far right, you can see the bodies are higher than the local ground surface. So the excavated grave was overfilled and there were bodies on the surface that were then covered by a bit of soil.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Okay. If the court officer can please turn to page 174 in e-court, still in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: This next picture is also from Cancari 12. It is labeled as a body part from that grave. Now the condition of this seems very different from the bodies that we just looked. Can you please explain how these are from the same grave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, I can talk generally about this point. When you have a pile of bodies in a clay grave, the bodies that are deep down are protected from oxygen, so they tend to putrefy much more slowly than bodies that are near the top of the grave. So much so that the -- that when we're looking at a single event of the disposal of bodies in a grave, the top layer of bodies may be skeletonised and the bodies underneath preserved like this. So the condition of a body in terms of its soft tissues is no guide to when it was -- was buried. You have to know the context within the grave of the particular body for that to be evaluated.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Just to be clear, when you say -- you've said, "When you're looking at a single event of the disposal of bodies," just in even more simplified terms, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Well, let us suppose that a grave is filled with bodies as a single event and then it's filled in. The bodies near the top will skeletonise rapidly. The bodies near the bottom will be -- have their soft tissue preserved because of the lack of oxygen for the bacteria to do their work.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 176 in e-court of the same exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And, Professor Wright, this is from a different grave-site, Hodzici 4. Can you please explain what we are looking at here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: We are looking at the front view of a human skull and there is a cloth that's tied around the area of the -- the nose. And you can just see above the cloth the -- half of the eye socket.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: When your team and you came across pieces of cloth like this or ligatures, would you remove them or would they remain on the bodies as they taken to the morgue?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No, we didn't remove them. We tried to disturb them as little as possible, clean up the body, clean up the cloth, but not remove the cloth. And then put the bodies in a body-bag. And then they went in a chiller van, they stayed in a chiller van until that was full, on the site, and then that was sent to the morgue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you. And we're going to turn now to a different report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If the court officer can bring up Exhibit 1761.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Professor Wright, this is your report on Kozluk. The Chamber has testimony that you've given about how you came to excavate Kozluk and they've also heard from Dean Manning a little bit about that so we'll just skip right to some of the results.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I'd like to look at page 22 in e-court in the English and page 23 in B/C/S. Actually, even -- there is a caption. It may be easier to only look at one screen to have it big enough. I've -- oh, actually the B/C/S does not have the figure. If there is no objection from the Defence, it may be easiest to just show the English version since it will be bigger in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you have no objections, I take it, against the suggestion? Please, it's there already.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: So, Professor Wright, this is a two-dimensional figure. And what I'm hoping you can do is explain the third dimension, the depth of the -- the significance about what these red dots are in the depth of the grave in addition to what we're seeing here in terms of the distribution of the red dots and the bodies. If you can also, if you understand what I mean, explain that distribution upon the layers of depth of the grave.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. We're looking here at a map produced by -- from our survey results, and you can see the individuals represented as stick figures. We're looking in the middle of that mass of bodies at -- bodies that lay on a slope, which was strewn with broken bottles, and the red dots represent our survey of the shell cases from ammunition, rifle ammunition, and they are mixed up with the bodies, but particularly common on the right hand side, top right hand side, particularly common on the edge of the slope on which the bodies lay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And just so that my question is clearly answered, when you say that the shell cases are "mixed up with the bodies," it's clear from this that they're at least on the top, but are they also mixed up throughout the depth of the grave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No, they are mixed up three-dimensionally with the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If we can please turn to page 30 in the English version in e-court and page 31 in B/C/S. Although, again, it may be best to keep the English version on the screen if that is okay with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one question. We saw a two-dimensional picture. Is there any computerised three-dimensional model made of what you found there? Because in the middle of it, it's all rather difficult to still identify what we see. It becomes a grey and black pudding more or less. That's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I did submit with this report a rotatable image which would have met the requirements you are asking about so that you could look at the bodies and the shell cases from any position by rotating the image.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So it does exist. Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. MacGregor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the top picture on the screen in front of you, this is also from the same KK3 grave. Now, you said in your report that you were unable to look for bullets in KK3 underneath bodies because of the substrate of bodies and glass. So I wonder if you can, using that picture as a guide, explain what you mean about your inability to look for bullets in this grave as compared to where you did in another part of Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. The -- we were able, of course, to find the shell cases, but the bullets were not embedded in the soil underneath these bodies. What we're looking at here is a view towards the slope that I mentioned, and in the background you can see the glass, the green glass from -- off the top of which we have already removed many bodies. So we're looking here at the few bodies that are at the base of the slope. And I don't recall finding bullets embedded in the soil in the same way as what we call -- as the area we called Kozluk 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Do you remember if you used the metal detector over the area underneath the bodies here in KK3?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I don't remember the event, but I'm pretty certain it would have been done, yes. It would have been done by Roland Wessling who was managing the metal detectors. But my mind doesn't -- I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If we can now look at page 29 in e-court, which is page 30 in the B/C/S. Again, just keeping the English version up as the picture. And actually if I can ask the court officer to zoom out to be able to show both pictures.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Now, this is a photograph you've explained of a man and he is holding something in his hand which you have identified as shrubby vegetation. Can you explain, is that vegetation rooted in that soil that is underneath the body?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, it's dead because it was covered up with bodies, but it's -- it's still in place but dead; in other words, yes, as you say, it is rooted in the clays -- in the silts at the base of the mass of bodies. And it's preserved, again, because of the lack of oxygen and the wetness of the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: We will now turn to your report on Glogova, Exhibit 1763. Now, as we're waiting for that to come up - and we'll be looking at page 38 in e-court in English, page 36 in B/C/S - you have described items in this report from the grave that led you to believe the grave was linked to Kravica warehouse. When had you been to the Kravica warehouse, before or after that excavation was completed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I originally went -- well, I was taken to the warehouse probably in 1998, but not with the intention of doing any work. The work was done in late 2000, and while I was doing the excavations at Glogova, I also visited the warehouse. In the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Again. And had the possible link between Kravica and Glogova been suggested to you already?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I imagine it had been but I can't remember the occasion on which it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And would that -- who would have suggested that to you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: It would have been the -- the investigators, I'm sure. I didn't -- I mean, I do recall knowing why I was asked to excavate the Glogova site but I cannot recall the occasion on which I was told or exactly what I was told. So the link with Kravica, yes, I was aware of that hypothesis.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And looking at the picture on the right in front of you, the top picture and the picture in the centre right, what are those pictures -- sorry, what are those of?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: They show excavations at the mass grave at Glogova and bits of what are interpreted as coming from the Kravica warehouse mixed up with the bodies, bits of the structure of the warehouse mixed up with the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Now, did you remove these materials?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Well, they were excavated, yes, and they were logged.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And do you know where they would have ended up?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Mike Hedley did a report on the warehouse and the relationship of the artefacts from the excavations to the warehouse, but I have no idea where the pieces went after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Did you discuss these items and what you found in the grave with Mr. Hedley?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, I went to the warehouse with Mr. Hedley to check the similarity between the items which we were excavating and what was down at the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And did you ever review his final report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I didn't see his final report until the other day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And when you say "the other day," do you mean in preparation for your testimony here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And once you were able to review it, did you draw any conclusions or form any opinions based on his report?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will -- was satisfied that my conclusions about the artefacts of Glogova were supported by his report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Now if we can turn to page 37 in e-court, which is page 35 in the B/C/S. For this picture, if I can again ask to just show the English version so that we are able to see the details of the paragraph. And if we can zoom in on the top photograph. Actually, that's great. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: So this one is a little harder to understand from a lay perspective. Can you explain the top photograph, what we're looking at, especially what the arrow is pointing at?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, we're looking at a shattered skull and that's made up of the white pieces. And then there is a piece of metal that I was told by the -- a piece of metal which is inside the skull, as it were, that I was told by an exploded ordinance advisor was a pellet from a grenade.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And if I can ask the court officer to scan down a bit to look at the two -- yes, thank you, those two pictures.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Now, the two pictures in the centre of the page, can you please explain how these -- what these are pictures of?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Well, this is a picture of the mummified flesh of a shoulder blade, of an area of the shoulder blade, and you can see on the left-hand one a piece of metal sticking out of a slit in the flesh. And on the right-hand side the archeologist has slid the piece of metal out of that slot, and I've forgotten what the metal was interpreted as but it was clearly embedded in the shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I mean, I don't know whether it was from a grenade or a shell, but it was a piece of metal that was forcibly -- and penetrated the shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And this condition of the human remains that you saw in the grave in Glogova, did you see that same type of damage to the bodies in other graves that you excavated?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I don't recall seeing that type of, what I'd call blast injury, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And thank you, I won't need this report any longer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Including your experiences outside of Bosnia -- sorry. I'm going to strike that question. In the past week the Chamber has heard a lot of questioning about whether bodies in these graves could have been battle casualties that were collected from the field and buried. Do you have any experience in exhuming graves that contained battle casualties?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I was the senior advisor to a team from Oxford Archeology that exhumed Australian soldiers from World War I. That was at a site called Fromelles in north-east France, and there were mass graves there and I saw the bodies in the grave. I didn't take part in their exhumation, but I saw the map that was produced subsequently and the bodies were laid across the graves in a -- in a respectable manner. I mean, respect had been shown to the dead in the disposition of these bodies. They were in rows and not just dumped in the graves.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And did you see anything in Bosnia -- in any of the exhumations that you did in Bosnia that was similar to that type of arrangement that you saw in Fromelles?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No, in the case of all the graves that I exhumed, the bodies were entangled, not laid out in rows, showed all the appearance of just having been dumped into the graves.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: -- I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have one follow-up question. The last question was whether you have any experience with battle casualties, and then you described how they were orderly buried in the north of France, and disorderly buried or dumped in the graves you inspected in Bosnia. Now does that say anything about whether these are battle casualties or does it say anything about the discipline of those who disposed of those bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I should have said, Your Honour, that the Australians were buried by the Germans, they were killed by the Germans when they made their way into the German trenches, and so the respectful burial was done by the enemy, not by the Australians themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether that's really an answer to my question. My question was battle casualties and -- compared to something you saw to be different here. Is the way in which people are buried a sufficiently strong indication of persons having died in battle circumstances, or does it say more about those enemies or -- from the same side, whether they were disciplined when burying the corpses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand now. I think I wouldn't care to generalise an answer, then. I was asked to comment on whether I had seen or taken part in the excavation of battle casualties and I described that one site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Not saying that this is -- would be an indication would be -- of course, it's different from what you saw in Bosnia, but you do not draw any conclusions as to whether the bodies disorderly buried in Bosnia would or would not have been battle casualties.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I couldn't -- I couldn't draw a conclusion from that alone, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic, we are close with the time -- at the time where we usually take a break. Perhaps it would be wisest to take the break first and that you would start your cross-examination after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we take the break first. Mr. Wright, may I invite you to follow the usher, and we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Welcome back, Mr. Wright. You'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. You'll find him to your left. You may proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Professor.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor Wright, could you please tell the Trial Chamber the following: In 1997, when you started working for the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, did you, and if so, how did you get information about the context of events in and about Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Well, in 1997 I was not involved in the Srebrenica investigations. I was at Brcko. But in 1998 I started working on the Srebrenica investigations. I was told why I was being employed and I was shown aerial images by the investigator which indicated where there might be graves, and I then decided which ones we could excavate because of logistical reasons of transport. And so I was given a general advice as to what I had to do and why I had to do it, and then I took over the actual excavations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who was the one who set up the team and determined the required expertise of persons who would work on excavations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: It was a joint discussion between myself and Mr. Jose Pablo Baraybar about the makeup of the team in 1998. In 1999 I -- in 1999 and 2000, I effectively chose the team from the list of people who had applied to an advertisement that ICTY published for experts, and I selected from that list.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true, sir, that there was a suggestion that no experts from former Yugoslavia, including Bosnia-Herzegovina, should be accepted to the team?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: That is my understanding, that that was the case, yes, and on the excavations themselves our equipment drivers were not local people. I didn't set that policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During your work on these projects of primary and secondary grave excavations, was local personnel involved in any way?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No, they weren't involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will kindly ask you to clarify some things to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, let us look at P1762. I hope that that's the correct number. Otherwise, it's 04602 on the 65 ter list. Could we please get both the English and the B/C/S versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 04602, Mr. Stojanovic, is P1761.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. It's my mistake. I need document P1761. Thank you, Your Honour. Could we please have page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor Wright, the way I understood the summary of your report, you say that at Kozluk you found three sites that you call mass graves. And they are KK1, KK2, and KK3. What is the reason for your considering these separate graves?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No, they were not separate graves. If I gave that impression on the previous page, then I'm wrong. They were areas of -- that we investigated. In the case of KK2, it was an area that contained some individuals lying on a surface, and in KK3 was the main area of bodies. But we were unable because of disturbance at the site to work out whether there were individual mass graves there, because the site had subsequently been excavated in October 1995. So KK1, KK2, and KK3 are areas of the Kozluk site that contained bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What is the difference between an individual grave and a mass grave according to the procedure you applied in your work?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: In the forensic literature, there is a lot of discussion about when -- how many individuals have to be present before a grave becomes a mass grave. We worked on the assumption that mass graves contained, obviously, more than one body, but in most cases we didn't have to worry about a definition because they were -- there were dozens of bodies and so no one would have argued with our use of the term "mass grave." I don't think there is a sensible definition of what is a mass grave as opposed to a grave with multiple burials, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now let us look at page 13 in the English and page 14 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain some things to us, sir. After listing detailed information about body parts and entire bodies found at Kozluk, you say that there were at least 451 --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please get the following page in both versions. It's continued over leaf. This is the paragraph in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You say that the total number of bodies is greater than 451 up to 660. What was the criterion based on which you determined the number of persons buried there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. In translation your word "determined" in English means that I have actually counted the number, but I have estimated the number of individuals that may have been at Kozluk, and my estimation is based on the -- can I see the previous page, because there are four propositions that I make and I just want to go and see the first one. Yes. There were 291 complete bodies that we actually excavated. Can we move onto the next page, now? We actually excavated them at Kozluk itself. And then we also recovered some body parts that were left over from the excavations of the grave that were done in October 1995 and we don't know how many individuals those body parts make up. And then we decided that Cancari 3, a secondary grave, and Cancari -- sorry, we decided that Cancari 3, according to the morgue, had 160 individuals, and we related Cancari 3 to Kozluk because of the green glass that was transferred across. And then there was another grave, Cancari 1, which has now been excavated but wasn't excavated by us. So I've assumed that that had the same order of numbers as Cancari 3; that is, Cancari 1 had the same order of numbers. And I've come up, then, with a very rough estimate that there may have been -- that there were more than 451 persons originally at the Kozluk site, and the maximum number might be in the order of 660. But it's not a determination. It's a very rough estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask you to explain the methodology you used in estimating the number of bodies at 660.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Well, in the case of Kozluk, I took the estimates -- or I took the estimates of the number of individuals at Kozluk itself from the figures I was given by the morgue. I didn't calculate them myself. And likewise with Cancari 3, I took count of the number of individuals determined at the morgue. Not by myself. And then I make an assumption that Cancari 1 has the same -- roughly the same number of individuals as Cancari 3, but that Cancari 1 had not been excavated, and that leads me to come up with a rough estimate of greater than 451 persons originally at the Kozluk site. So we know from the morgue how many individuals we exhumed from the Kozluk site, but we know that they were -- they were transferred to Cancari 1 and Cancari 3 on the basis of the artefacts that were found at Cancari 1 and Cancari 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you one question. When you say a complete body was exhumed, you mean a complete body, everything being present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it may be that a hand will not be present, but it is essentially a body where you would have to look carefully to see what parts might be missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which means that if the hand was found somewhere else in the same area or same grave, may have been counted in your estimate that there were more people buried there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ah --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said parts, body parts, if they were found. So is there a risk of counting double by finding that hand, well, let's say, somewhere else but it's still in the same grave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will -- I will remember I was not doing the counting. The morgue was doing the counting. Now, the morgue would not have counted a hand as an individual, I am confident, but I don't know their actual procedures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but you are also referring to -- you are referring to complete bodies found and body parts found. Now, could it be that the almost complete body, with a body part being a hand, that the hand would have played a role in your further estimates that there were more people buried there than the number of complete bodies found?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I -- the answer to that is the morgue received what we thought were complete bodies and had filled out a body sheet for that body. They also received the body parts. And so I was not part of the process of the analysis of body parts, and that's why I am -- in that paragraph I express an uncertainty about the very point you're raising.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Professor. I would like to show a document now. That's why I asked these questions. It is from the P4181, collection, page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if you remember, Your Honours, it's a map compiled by a witness we were able to hear last week. It's an investigator who compiled it, this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the map to upload, let me ask you once again, sir, whether that means that in this rough estimate of yours of up to 660 bodies in the primary site at Kozluk --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Defence counsel please repeat the latter part of his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, could you please repeat the latter part of the your question which was not caught by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly? In your rough estimate of up to 660 bodies, in the primary site at Kozluk, whether that includes an estimate of the possible number of bodies in the secondary site CR1, which is Cancari 1?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, it did explicitly in the sections we looked at previously include that -- an estimate for what might be in Cancari 1. Since then, Cancari 1 has been excavated, not by myself, and I don't offhand know how many bodies they did find.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What confuses me, sir, is this map. Can you please focus on its central part, and let us enlarge it, especially the area from Kozluk to the green marks near Cancari. According to this map made by Dean Manning, the investigators think that the secondary sites of Cancari 3, as you said, and Cancari 2, are related to the primary site at Kozluk, whereas on this map there is no relation between Cancari 1 and the primary site at Kozluk. Can you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, I can see -- indeed, I can see what you're saying, and I don't know what the explanation is, whether I have got the title of the grave with green glass incorrect, but I'd have to look at my report to see whether I relate Cancari 1 or Cancari 2 with the green glass. That is in my 1999 report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps you can help us with that during the next break. Let me now ask you if you remember whether any other, apart from these two secondary sites marked as Cancari Road, is related to the primary site at Kozluk based on artefacts or anything else?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No, I don't recall seeing other secondary sites that I could relate to Kozluk.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber if you took part in the exhumation of any other secondary site at Cancari Road except for Cancari 3?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, I conducted the exhumations at Cancari 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And you will agree with me, won't you, that it had to do with the events around Branjevo and not Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: That, as I understand it, is how the soil analyses pointed, yes. When we excavated Cancari 12, I noticed that soils mixed up with the bodies did not look like local soils, and so Dr. Tony Brown was called in to provide an expert analysis, and I know from his report that he relates Cancari 12 to a grave at Branjevo farm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of the fact that you were heading the project, do you remember -- do you know whether it was established that after the DNA analysis there is a part -- a body part in the primary grave in Kozluk and that same part of the -- or another part of the same body would be found in the secondary grave, Cancari 3?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of the DNA results. They were done long after I finished the excavations and I was not part of the team that -- that analysed those results.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, am I wrong if I see in the previous testimony of the witness that he describes the particles of green glass in the Cancari Road 3, which would be fully consistent, but it's apparently they're not consistent with the -- with the red line on a map which this witness has not created. So is -- this map is made, I think, after the witness had done his job because he says Cancari 1 was not exhumed by him. So therefore apparently there is new information at a later stage, and there may be mistakes there, but is it for this witness to answer those questions or is it for the person who drafted this map? That's my -- I mean, to put a confusion to the witness where he may be totally foreign to that confusion might be a bit problematic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour. I will not be using the map anymore. But I must admit that I accept that the artefact of glass in Cancari 3 is directly linked to the primary grave-site in Kozluk. I think that the previous witness also spoke about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although the red lines suggest something different on the map. But let's not bother this witness with possible mistakes, and I have to reread it all to see whether there really are any mistakes or not. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, the next thing that I would like to ask you is this: In the context of the events that have to do with the Kozluk primary grave, were you informed whether the victims in Kozluk were brought to the execution place, and if so, where they were brought from?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I don't remember being told that. I should, perhaps, expand a moment on the discovery of the Kozluk primary site. It came about because at Cancari 3, where we found all this green glass, we had to explain why there were these thousands of pieces of broken glass in this grave, and we found labels with the broken glass and with the bodies that gave the name of the Vitinka bottling factory at Kozluk, and it was only after that that the primary site of Kozluk was found on which I worked. That was in 1998 we discovered it and in 1999 I exhumed it. I don't remember being told anything about where the -- the -- the people killed at Kozluk had come from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if I understand you well, even not whether they were killed at Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I missed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, you said you did not receive any information where the people came from who were killed at Kozluk.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I do even understand that do you not even know whether they were killed at Kozluk. They were buried in the primary grave in Kozluk, or?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have my opinions that they were shot at Kozluk because of the number of shell cases, hundreds of shell cases that were found with the bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And now this question regarding your opinion as to the place of execution of the victims. Sticking to the rules of your profession, would you be able to say if all of those bodies in Kozluk were executed and died there or were there dead bodies that were brought to that site and then buried there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: My conclusion is that because of the way the bodies were lying on the ground and because of the number of shell cases that were at the site, that people were killed there. I don't pretend to say that all of them were killed there, others might have been brought in already dead and mixed up with the bodies. But because of the state of preservation of these bodies, if dead bodies were brought in and buried it would have been at the same time as the shootings of the others took place. So I would not conclude that every body that we found was killed there, but everybody was killed at the same time in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I'm asking you this because according to the indictment, and our theory of the case, those people were brought from the school in Rocevic, as stated in the indictment, but also there were some executions in front of the school as well. And so I wanted to ask you whether in your work you ever had any information about the place where the bodies of people were buried of victims who were executed or killed in front of the school in Rocevic.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that -- that name. And can I ask are we talking about Kozluk only or about the graves in general?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was asking you about the grave-site in Kozluk, Professor. And thank you for the answer. I would now want to ask you whether it's correct that those pieces of glass found in the secondary site, Cancari 3, which correspond to the glass fragments found at the primary site in Kozluk, were not preserved?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, were not preserved by the -- by ICTY? Was that -- I -- I'm sure we collected some samples of glass from both sites, but I was not responsible for the continuity of the evidence after that. Once I had delivered the evidence, I was not responsible for preservation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't doubt that, Professor, but I wanted to ask you if you know whether these artefacts, the glass was preserved anywhere now and whether they could be subjected to a fresh analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I see. No, I don't know whether that can happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, now I would like to look at 65 ter 04603. I think that that would be the right number. I think that would be P7162 [as interpreted]. I wouldn't want to make a mistake with the numbers. So could we have that in e-court, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1762. Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Could we please look at page 34 together. That's the English version. And then page 36 of the B/C/S version of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, could you please explain to us a little bit this estimate that you made which resulted in this number, 3.474 bodies?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us the methodology that you used in order to get to this figure and this estimate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I think the report describes how it was done, so if you would have any focused question on where you apparently do not understand it, it is about average numbers of graves of a certain size and then extrapolated to the number. It seems to be relatively clearly explained, so if you have any focused question that would also show where your problems are. Witness, unless I'm mistaken, if I misread your report, please tell me at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I agree, Your Honour, that the methodology is set out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The -- there is additional information because the -- the graves that I talk about as probed unexcavated graves have now been excavated, and an ICTY document by -- I think it's Mr. Dusan gives the numbers of bodies of 19 of those 21 graves and my estimate was a slight underestimate based on those 19 graves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the way you worked with the knowledge at the time is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- relatively clearly explained in the report, I would say. So therefore, Mr. Stojanovic, why ask the witness -- please show us where you do not understand it or where you have doubts and ask the witness about that rather than to repeat again what he has already written in his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Well, why am I asking this? It's for the following reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, when you completed your work and once you completed this report, do you stand by this number of 857 as the definite number that you established following your work? Everything that is above that amounts to an estimate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: It was an estimate. Any number above 857, which I derived from the staff at the morgue, was when I wrote the report an estimate. But now the graves have been excavated, there are counts of the numbers of bodies in 19 of those 21 unexcavated graves. And, as I said to the President, those numbers show that I slightly underestimated the number of bodies in the unexcavated graves by about 10 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 65 ter 04611, please. I think this is P1763. Could we look at page 3 of the B/C/S and the English versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, this is a report that you did on the excavation of the Glogova 1 grave-site. I wanted to ask you this: Was Glogova 1 one single grave or did it consist of several sites?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: It consisted of several distinct graves, distinctly dug holes. But in the main area of Glogova 1, because it had been disturbed in October 1995, we were not able to work out whether it was all one single grave or a series of individual graves. So I can't answer -- I can answer your question for the fringes of the site that there were several individual graves, but I can't tell you how many individual graves there were in the main area of excavation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: All of those graves, were they all disturbed in October 1995 as you said?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No, they weren't all disturbed. Those on the -- I do have, Your Honour, a map of the site, and it would be easier to answer it from the map, to answer the question from the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean the map as part of your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stojanovic, if this is ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think he's referring to figure 4 in that report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which is found at page?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I would have -- the page number is around 25. I'd have to hunt a bit once we're there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 24 gives a map and it's perhaps not as detailed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Page 28 I am told by Ms. Stewart. It's a schematic rather than a street -- or road map like this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I wanted to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And thank you to the Prosecution for their help.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, could you please tell us, when you see this map, are you able to tell us which graves were desecrated and attacked in October 1995 as you said?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. The -- if we start from the top, all of the graves - that's grave F, grave C, grave H, and grave K - were disturbed in October 1995, but grave E and L were not disturbed. So those two - those are at the bottom of the image and to the right, grave E and grave L - were not disturbed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief today, you said, among other things, that this grave-site is something that you connect to the events at the Kravica warehouse. In view of the artefacts that were found in these grave-sites, Glogova 1, I wanted to ask you whether that would indicate or could indicate that all the bodies found in these graves in Glogova 1 came from the Kravica warehouse?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Again, as with my answer about Kozluk, I don't believe that it shows that all the bodies came from the Kravica warehouse, but it indicates that when -- that bodies from the Kravica warehouse were brought to the site with parts of the broken door brought with the bodies, but I -- I would accept a proposition that some of the bodies may have come from somewhere else. I don't claim that all the bodies there were brought from the Kravica warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you please tell us, Professor, your work or the work of some other experts at the Visoko morgue, did it help to establish the time of death, approximate time of death of all 190 victims whose bodies were found at the Glogova 1 site?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: May I ask, do you mean the year of death? Are we talking about the time of day or the time of -- the year, which year? I don't -- I don't know the answer to any of those questions anyway because I was not concerned with the work that was done at the morgue. We formed at the site our opinions about the simultaneous burials, but I don't know what conclusions the morgue arrived at that were -- agreed with us or disagreed with us about the time of death. And I doubt very much whether the morgue would be able to determine in what year the individuals died other than by the same information that we had which were -- look at documents and at the aerial images of the disturbances in October 1995 and the original disturbance of the burials in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I was just waiting for the interpretation to finish. I want to ask you this also: Were you present when Glogova L was being excavated as the primary grave? Were you personally present during the excavation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, I was personally present and I was in charge of that excavation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, could you please tell me if you received information, and from whom you received information, about another grave that needed to be checked in the village of Potocari?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Potocari is -- is a village near Srebrenica. It's -- it's where the bus station was. Yes, I did go to -- I --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I did go to that site and we found a hole in the ground, but we did not find bodies in the hole. I think that year was 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I take you back to one of your previous answers. You told us about which graves were disturbed when looking at this map, and you refer to E and L as the non-disturbed graves at the bottom, and you included K in one of the disturbed graves. Now if I look at your report -- let me see. I read, unless I'm -- let me just check one second, please. For Glogova 1, I read on page 6: "Grave K, an intact primary grave, not robbed." The same for L. Is there any chance that you may have mixed up E and K because --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I just had a lapse of memory then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stojanovic, if someone has written a report, then to ask him to reproduce by heart what is clearly described in the report doesn't make much sense during cross-examination, unless I'm looking at the wrong report but we are still talking about Glogova 1? Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, are you aware that close to Kravica and Glogova was where the 28th Division was moving as it was breaking through from Kravica towards Tuzla? And this was in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, before you ask these details, we should first ask whether the witness has any knowledge about military movements and who moved where and when.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't have any coherent knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much. Then I would not dwell on that topic anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I do want to ask you, though, whether during the time you spent in this area in Kravica, Glogova, did you have any information as to whether the terrain was sanitised in that area and whether all the bodies that -- of people that were killed during combat were collected and taken away?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No, I was not told. I was not told that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Now I'm going to move to topics that have to do with the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I think that perhaps at this time, Your Honours, would be a good time to go on a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I'd like to ask one additional question. In your work, excavations, exhumations, did you find any indication that the persons buried in the graves you examined, that they would have been bodies of persons which may have collected -- been collected somewhere on the terrain as battle casualties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I got no such indications. As you asked me the question, I'm thinking: What would I be looking for. All I saw were -- all the bodies I saw were dressed in civilian clothing, so without knowing historical background, my initial reaction to that would be that these were civilians. Whether they'd been collected from the landscape, I would expect them to be in different stages of decomposition before they were put into the grave, and I would expect to see the remains of insects with the bodies, and we didn't find such evidence in the -- in these graves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To understand the last part of your answer, the insects, are you referring to insects which would have already, if I could say so, attacked or at least entered into the bodies and then be taken together with the bodies, if in this hypothesis, then to be taken to the grave where people were buried and then still be with those bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I think that was the issue you wanted to raise, not whether the witness has any knowledge but whether the witness has found anything which would either support or would not support or even contradict the hypothesis. We'll take a break. You may follow the usher. We'd like to see you back in approximately 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and will resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I would like to briefly raise a matter. The Defence had asked for an enlargement of time, two weeks, until the 23rd of July, to respond to the motion, which by the way I see is a confidential motion but to add witnesses.
