Is there any objection against an extension of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Lukic, the time you have to respond to that motion is extended with 14 days so that the response is now due the 23rd of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you're ready, Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could we please see 1D1139, pages 66 and 67 respectively. It's the Karadzic transcript, and I'm interested in the last paragraph on page 305.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please listen carefully to the question I'm about to ask, and then we'll -- actually, that was asked -- that was put to you. And then I would like to move on to page 306. While you're reading, in the Karadzic case you were asked if you could rule out the possibility that the bodies at Glogova were buried as part of the sanitizing process and you answered that you couldn't rule that out completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, where are you reading? We would like to keep up with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I believe that I'm interested in the first paragraph, the answer on page 22306. It's what we have on our screens, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We don't see the question that you say was put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission I will go back to page 66 in e-court or 22305. Here's the question as put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, Professor, if you still stand by the answer you provided in the Karadzic case.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we move onto the next page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do stand by that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D1139 is hereby tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's 75 pages, Mr. Stojanovic. You've dealt with one or two pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. It's just pages 66 and 67 of this transcript as I've stated already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But then you have to upload it as a separate exhibit. We'll reserve a number for those pages. Madam Registrar, the number to be reserved for that would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number reserved for the two pages of document 1D1139 will be D331, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more clarification, Professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, was -- what has it added to the previous question? I mean, I asked the witness about whether he found indications. He said, "Well, you would expect to find insects, et cetera," but he never said that he would have excluded anything definitely. What now does this add? He did not exclude it in the previous question, either, did he? He just said that it would be an indication that it might not be bodies which had been left out on the terrain and then collected later. Even the witness says he has no reason to believe that they were. But what now does this add to the previous answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why do we need to have it in evidence, those pages? He explains exactly the same thing as he did in the last question -- series of questions, whether people were wearing military uniforms or not. He already said, "I don't know anything about the background," could mean nothing -- could be not -- he doesn't express himself on in it. And the insects he said would be an indication to the contrary of this. What now does this add?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm about to tackle the issue of insects, therefore I wanted this explicit answer provided by Professor Wright to be in evidence and now I want to deal with the witness's argument with relation to insects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not mind if you want to go further in detail with the insects, but I am concerned about you tendering a not-yet-prepared 75 pages and then reduce it to two pages which brings us nothing new. The only thing, the difference is that he was a little bit more in detail talking about blowflies and the chitinous material of their bodies and wings. That's the only detail which is added which is hereby on the record. So I don't think, Madam Registrar, that we need to have a number reserved for the not-yet-uploaded portion of the previous testimony. Please proceed, including if with your insects. Madam Registrar, therefore, the reserved number it's not attached yet to an uploaded document. This is hereby vacated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, preparing for today's examination I had the opportunity to read a number of transcripts. When Professor Lawrence was examined in the Karadzic case, he said - I'm paraphrasing now - that after three years, a significant amount of evidence belonging to forensic entomology would have been destroyed, would have disappeared beyond reconstruction. He was referring to something that you mentioned as a possible basis for drawing conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the Prosecutor objects, I would add that this is page 22465 in Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And now I'll ask you whether you would agree with Professor Lawrence's statement, if he made such a statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. MacGregor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would just ask that if we're going to ask Professor Wright to comment on the testimony of someone else, first of all that he be given a full name and perhaps the area that that other person is an expert in just in case -- so we have the record clear but also so that this witness clear, and then we can determine if he's in fact in a position to comment on that statement by another expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's one. And second, by just giving a page number to Mr. Wright who may have no idea what is to be found on that page seems not to be the appropriate way of proceeding. If you want to put this to Mr. Wright, then you have to give him at least the full details. And perhaps he knows the author, I do not know. Perhaps that's the first question you would ask him, whether he knows Professor Lawrence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I do know Professor Lawrence, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So therefore, qualifications, Ms. MacGregor, seems not to be -- I take it that you know him from your professional background and you're --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- aware of his qualifications.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He -- yes, I do. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Stojanovic, if you want to put any conclusions by Professor Lawrence to this witness, then you have to do that in detail and very precise because otherwise we can't expect this witness to meaningfully comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The witness will be heard until the end of the week.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you, sir, that after three years - that is, three years after the burial - it is difficult to establish using the means of forensic entomology the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The interpreters were unable to hear or understand you, Mr. Stojanovic. But let's leave Professor Lawrence for a moment alone. When you said it would have been a -- you would have expected any insects' remains with the bodies to be found, have you taken into account the time and have you considered to what extent evidence of the presence of insects would have faded away or would have disappeared over a number of years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My answer is that I'm, of course, not an expert in forensic entomology, but in my own experience and in Bosnia at the site of Kevljani, we found insect remains on bodies that were believed to have dated from 1992 and we were working, I think, in 1997. And so we found in -- I have seen personally insect remains. But as to a general account of where they survive, the soil conditions and so on, I am not an expert. But I do know from forensic reading that I have done that insect remains will last for many years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. May I correct the date? It was not 1997. It was 1998 or 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- because earlier you corrected -- when a question was put to you about 1997, you said it was 1998.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Work at Kevljani was done in 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for the correction. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us stick to the Kevljani report. 11409 is the number on the 65 ter list. I'm afraid --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document P1764, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has been admitted meanwhile.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let us look at page 3 in both linguistic versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The first thing I would like to ask you, Professor, is the following: On page 2 you say that you found 72 complete bodies in 15 virtually intact graves. Then you estimate that in the remaining disturbed and removed bodies -- or, rather, that the number of such bodies is 72 again. I would like to know which methodology you used to establish that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: May I first say that my memory is worse than I thought. It was 1999 that I worked at Kevljani.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Add another few years, Mr. Wright, and we come to 2013. Yes. No --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thought that -- in -- in answer to your question, can we look at the map that is included in my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, could you guide us to the map. And I think in general asking questions about the summary seems not to be the best thing to do where the witness has explained in his report quite a number of things which do not appear in similar detail in the summary.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. MacGregor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you switch on your microphone?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Is it on? There is a figure 2 that I think is page 17 that may be -- it's a schematic map. I think it may be that one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one I want. Now, my answer depends on our knowledge that there were two major rows of graves; one row which was largely undisturbed at the top, and then a row of graves to the right of them which were largely disturbed but covered the same sort of distance and area. And then there are two -- in the bottom left-hand side, there are two disturbed graves and two undisturbed graves. So we know how many bodies were found in the undisturbed graves and that estimate - and I repeat it is an estimate - of 72 makes the assumption that the same sort of area is covered in the disturbed graves from which the bodies were taken away. So 72 is -- for the undisturbed areas and the partly disturbed graves is a count, and the other number 72 that I mention is an estimate based on the assumption that we're looking at the same sort of area of disturbed graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, do you think that this is a primary burial site or a secondary one?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: We formed the opinion that it was a primary burial site. The bodies were in an intact state. There were some body parts but we interpreted them as left over from the disturbance at the site, but that the undisturbed graves were places of primary burial.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you this because I wanted you to assist us. That being the case, do you think that the bodies and persons buried there were killed at that very site or were they brought there already dead?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I think they were brought there already dead on the grounds that we didn't find numerous shell cases such as we did, say, at Kozluk. We saw no evidence of signs of execution at that spot. So I think they were brought there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By the way, Mr. Stojanovic, again, the way in which the witness has estimated or on what basis of what kind of calculation he has based his estimates are found in the report in detail. Therefore, why ask him again about methodology which is -- I mean, let's try to focus on what really matters and not put the same question to the witness and then accept the same answer. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, the fact that in a number of graves iron ore was found, could that be an indication of where the bodies in question had been brought from?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. And Dr. Brown was brought in to analyse these foreign rocks, foreign rocky material that we found in these graves. It consisted of some piece of slag which is left over from a furnace, and it consisted of some pieces of raw iron ore. And so a report was written by Dr. Brown who visited the site, and he concluded that that material was consistent with the bodies having been brought from the site at Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us look at 1D123.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D123 is not in e-court, Your Honour. Could it be 1123?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I apologise. 1123. I would like to see page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, during the excavation of the Kevljani burial site, was local personnel from Bosnia-Herzegovina also involved?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You asked this question earlier today, Mr. Stojanovic, and the Professor said no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. That related to the exhumations relating to Srebrenica, and this one has to do with a site in the Krajina area and that was the reason for my question because now I'm about to mention the name of a local site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, so my question was: Do you recall if the exhumations in Krajina, specifically in Kevljani, included local personnel from Bosnia and Herzegovina also?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No, there were no locals taking part in the exhumation. Just can I -- I'm not sure what the purpose of your question is, but can I just anticipate this by saying that people would have been able to observe our exhumations but they certainly didn't take part in the exhumations. We were in the -- there were roads passing close and so they could have observed what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Well, the question is now if you know whether any of the local staff took part in the process of processing and identifying of the bodies?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: The identifications were certainly not my responsibility and no one came to the site for the purpose of attempting to identify the individuals. I mean, no local people came to the site to do any work whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to ask you something about the document. Does the name Jasmin Odobasic mean anything to you, who at the time was the chief of the federal commission for searching for missing persons in 2005? Did you have the opportunity to meet this person at any point during your work?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I don't remember meeting such a person, and I -- my work finished in Bosnia in 2000. But I don't -- no, I don't remember meeting such a person.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at paragraph 30 of this statement which the then-chief of the federal commission for missing persons gave to the international tribunal and to the investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to just put a couple of questions to you, Professor, so perhaps you can help. In paragraph 30 the witness says, among other things: "Let me just mention one problem: In 1999, the ICTY exhumed a mass grave - Kevljani, a secondary grave - with 143 bodies. Eva Klonowski and Nermin Sarajlic processed these bodies. And they made mistakes there as well. An example is the identification of Mursija Zenkic. In 2004, I exhumed another secondary grave, Stari Kevljani, just 200 metres away from the first grave. 456 bodies were exhumed, all camp inmates from Omarska. Among those bodies, I found the body of Mursija Zenkic with her identity papers. Physician Ana Boza was in charge of the onsite examination of the bodies, but later during the final autopsy and the identification process of the ICMP replaced her with Eva Klonowski and Nermin Sarajlic and she was literally excluded from the whole process." My question is this: After you left this locality, up to 2000, was the final number of persons linked with that grave-site ever established?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Well, I had nothing to do with the processing of the bodies and the identifications. My understanding was that the -- the bodies from Kevljani, which was a primary grave, in my opinion, not a secondary grave, that the bodies were taken to the ICTY morgue for examination. And I don't understand the remainder of that paragraph, maybe because I'm just ignorant of what happened, but I couldn't answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And I'm going to finish with this question, Professor: Did you, in your work in any way, respecting the rules of your profession, establish that these were the bodies of persons who were detained in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No, it was not my business to do that. And it was my business to draw attention to items of material culture and of rocks which might bear on the question of where these people had come from, but my brief did not go beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Ms. MacGregor, is there any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I do have one question for the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please put that question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I just want to clarify the Professor's testimony before on the comments of Dr. Lawrence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And to be clear, we're talking about Dr. Christopher Lawrence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And what was his role on these exhumations you worked with him on?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: He didn't have a role in the exhumations. He was -- he was, in 1998, in charge of the operations at the morgue, though he did visit the exhumations but he had no -- no role in the exhumations in any official sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Was he the chief pathologist of the project?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: That was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you. So I've located the quote from Dr. Lawrence's Karadzic testimony, and I will just -- since we don't all have it in front of us, I will slowly read the question and answer and just ask you, based on your experience in the forensic work you've done, if you would agree or not with his conclusion. The question: "Q. Would the presence of insects give any kind of indication as to the time that the body was there, from the time of death to the time of burial? "A. Sorry, yes. If they were present, it could be helpful. I think my experience with forensic entomology suggests to me that sometimes it's helpful and sometimes it's not. It doesn't always work. I also suspect that after three years quite a lot of the forensic entomology evidence would have gone and would not be recoverable." And did you need me to repeat the question that I asked to you, Professor Wright?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I can only talk about my own experience, and at Kevljani, it lasted longer than three years. But I absolutely decline to be drawn into discussions about forensic entomology in general.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one further question. On the same subject, is Professor Lawrence known to you - and I'm not asking you to disqualify him - as a specialist in forensic entomology.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he's known to me as a medical pathologist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any further questions, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Stojanovic, I haven't heard you about the need for further time to prepare further cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. In view of your suggestion, we did prepare for Kevljani and these other two locations so there is no need to recall Professor Wright on these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that information. I asked this, Mr. Wright, because there had been a discussion about whether there would be any need to recall you since some of the reports were -- were presented rather late as to be dealt with during your examination, but luckily enough, you don't have to travel again. At least not for us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because we have concluded your evidence. I'd like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you either by the parties or by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher and you are excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would the Prosecution be ready to call its next witness? I'm not yet asking you to do, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: My understanding is that we are prepared, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because there are a few other matters on our agenda as well, and since we are -- we may have some time to do that. But let me just try to get organised again. First I'd like to deal with one procedural matter, which is 92 ter motions for upcoming expert witnesses. For a number of upcoming expert witnesses, the Prosecution has filed Rule 92 ter motions tendering transcript portions as well as expert reports as associated exhibits. In this respect, the Chamber recalls its decision on the Prosecution 92 ter motion concerning Witness Teufika Ibrahimefendic, dated the 1st of July, 2013, and will consider those documents filed pursuant to Rule 92 ter of the Rules as Rule 94 bis documents. Then there are a few decisions which I would like to render. There are a few. There are four. I'd like to use the next minutes for that. I'll start with the ones which can be delivered in open session. But if you would just bear with me for one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just wanted to make sure that the booth had received all of the decisions. The first one is an oral decision on the amalgamated witness statement and associated exhibits of Witness Rupert Smith. By its confidential decision issued on the 28th of June, 2013, the Chamber decided that there is no need to recall Witness Smith. It is hereby put on the public record that the testimony of Witness Smith is concluded. The Chamber will now turn to its outstanding decision on the admission of his amalgamated witness statement of the 22nd of October, 2009, which is currently marked for identification as Exhibit P785 as well as the remaining associated exhibits to it. At first, following the conclusion of his testimony before the Tribunal, the Chamber admits Witness Smith's amalgamated witness statement of the 22nd October 2009, currently marked for identification as Exhibit P785, and it's admitted into evidence. With regard to the outstanding associated exhibits, the Chamber notes at the outset that it was not properly guided as to which associated exhibit is referred to in different parts of the witness statement because the statement itself refers to document ID numbers, whereas the Rule 92 ter exhibit list, as provided by the Prosecution, refers to Rule 65 ter numbers of the respective exhibits. In addition, many references to document ID numbers in the statement proved to be incorrect and the Chamber was only able to find the corresponding associated exhibit by carefully analysing the affected sections together with the associated exhibits. Therefore, in order to avoid this in the future, the Chamber requests the Prosecution to clearly set out the corresponding paragraphs in the relevant witness statement for each associated exhibit it seeks to be incorporated into its Rule 92 ter exhibit list. Following the Chamber's approach in the Tucker oral decision of the 22nd of November, 2012, on the admission of associated exhibits, the Chamber admits the following 12 documents into evidence as associated exhibits through the witness -- to the statement of Witness Smith. Rule 65 ter numbers 03500, 11469, 03503, 05727, 05728, 19262, 05832, 05589, 18635, 17475, 08946, and 03502. With regard to Rule 65 ter number 09670, the Chamber notes that it has not been able to find its corresponding paragraph or section in the witness statement. In the event that the Prosecution still intends to have this document admitted, it is hereby invited to inform the Chamber of the correct reference in order to enable the Chamber to decide on its admission. With regard to the remaining 19 associated exhibits tendered by the Prosecution through Witness Smith, the Chamber denies their admission into evidence without prejudice. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. I move to the next decision which relates to Exhibit P1003. This is the Chamber's decision on the admission of Exhibit P1003 into evidence. During the testimony of Witness Nermin Karagic on the 21st of February of this year, the Prosecution used a comments chart which, when tendered for admission into evidence, was marked for identification as Exhibit P1003. At the direction of the Trial Chamber, the parties made further submissions on the chart on the 1st of March, 2013. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: (redacted) The Prosecution submitted that the Defence's objection was a question of the weight to be attributed to the chart. And these submissions can be found at transcript page 9509. The Chamber has analysed the comments chart in light of Rules 89(C) and (D) of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence and notes at the outset that the evidence relates to Scheduled Incidents A 6.7, A 6.8, and C 15.5. The Chamber observed that Witness Karagic prepared the comments chart prior to his testimony in court, recalling what happened to the persons listed therein based on his knowledge. The witness also made additional comments in court and affirmed the document's authenticity. This can be found at transcript pages 9106 to 9109. In the comments the witness clearly indicated those persons he knew personally and any uncertainty he had about the identity and/or fate of persons. Considering this, the Chamber finds the comments chart to be prima facie relevant and to have probative value of Scheduled Incidents A 6.7, A 6.8, and C 15 of the indictment, and therefore admits P1003 into evidence. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. The next decision is the decision on the Prosecution motion to amend its 65 ter witness list to substitute Witness RM705 with Witness RM095. On the 9th of May, 2013, the Prosecution filed a confidential motion seeking leave to add Witness RM095 to its Rule 65 ter list as a proposed Rule 92 bis witness in substitution of proposed 92 bis Witness RM705 whom the Prosecution seeks to withdraw. The Prosecution submits that the substitution of witnesses will not cause prejudice to the Defence because the expected evidence covers the topic of alleged detention and killing in Prijedor. The Prosecution submits that it has good cause for the substitution considering what the Defence has recently described as its "revenge" defence and Witness RM705's reluctance to have their evidence used in any form due to personal security concerns. The Defence filed its response on the 23rd of May objecting to the substitution on the ground that the Prosecution failed to establish good cause. The Chamber considers that the Prosecution has not shown good cause for adding Witness RM095 to its Rule 65 ter witness list. However, considering Witness RM705's reluctance to provide evidence because of personal security concerns, and considering that the anticipated evidence of both witnesses is substantially similar, thereby causing limited additional burden for the Defence, the Chamber finds that it is in the interest of justice to allow substitution, and for these reasons the Chamber grants the motion. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. Although I would have one more decision to be delivered, I refrain from that because the next witness is scheduled for chief -- in chief for half an hour. We'll see at the end of today's session whether still time remains before cross-examination will start to read that last decision. Ms. MacGregor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: (redacted) may I remind the Prosecution that it's appropriately done in private session. We take a break. And, Ms. MacGregor, the Chamber expects that examination-in-chief can be concluded today.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe it can. It's Mr. Jeremy who will be handling the next witness so he can answer to that, but I believe he can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have the same expectations as far as he's concerned. We take the break and will resume at 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness please put on the earphones, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you by the usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Maljaars, you'll first be examined by Mr. Jeremy. Mr. Jeremy is counsel for the Prosecution and you'll find him to your right. You may proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Maljaars.

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could I start by stating your full name for the record, please?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: Suzanna Elisabeth Maljaars.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And I see you've brought some materials in with you to the courtroom. Could you briefly tell the Court what those are, please.

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: It's a copy of a report that I wrote in February 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you to make a short pause --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- between question and answer because your second name has already disappeared from the transcript. It was Suzanna Elisabeth Maljaars. Could you please keep this in mind, both.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Ms. Maljaars, what is your current profession?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: My current profession is a chemistry teacher.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And could you briefly tell us about your educational background, the main points.

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: I finished laboratory school and later on I finished university, both in chemistry. And after I finished chemistry in university, I followed a post programme, post-doc programme to become a chemistry teacher.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honours, could I please see 65 ter 29089 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And while that's coming up, Ms. Maljaars, do you recall providing a copy of your CV to the Office of the Prosecutor in the past?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And I see in the -- the title below your names it says "drs." which I understand is a Dutch term, "doctorandus," that indicates that you have a master's degree rather than a PhD; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And is the information contained in this CV accurate as at 2003? Does it outline the courses you attended, your professional employment, and the publications you had written up until 2003?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tender that as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 29089 receives number P1770, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Ms. Maljaars, your CV states that, by the year 2000, you'd been employed by the Netherlands Forensic Institute for approximately ten years; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And could you very briefly explain what the Netherlands Forensic Institute is?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: The Netherlands Forensic Institute is an institute that conducts forensic investigations for the whole of the Netherlands, and it is specialising in all types of forensic investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And is one of the areas that it specialises in textiles investigations?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And has the Netherlands Forensic Institute, or NFI for short, previously provided a report relating to your analysis of textiles material, a report specifically prepared by you to the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: Yes, they have.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we please see 65 ter 04612 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Ms. Maljaars, do you recognise the document on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And I see the subject of the document is "Textile Investigation," it's dated 11 February, 2000. Can you very briefly explain to the Court what this document is, please?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: This document is a report that I wrote concerning textile investigations on pieces of textiles that I have received, and I was asked to look for similarities between the pieces of textile.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And from -- from whom did you receive those pieces of textile?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: We received them from Mr. Ruez, Mr. Kruszewski, and Mr. Manning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please go to page 24 in the English and page 23 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Ms. Maljaars, in the English version on the right-hand side of the screen we see a signature. Whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: It is mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And before your name below this signature I see "Ing," what does that represent?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: That's a short version of "engineer," and that's my bachelor degree in chemistry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So does that reflect your level of education at the time that you wrote this report?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And what was your position within the Netherlands Forensic Institute when you prepared and wrote this report?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: I was a research co-ordination -- co-ordinator for the hair, fibre, and textile investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And what did that mean in -- in practice in respect to reports like this?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: It meant that I conducted investigations on textiles in a forensic way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And at the time of writing this report, had you completed any relevant publications related to this field of expertise?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: In 1991 I co-wrote a publication about fibres and their evidence in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And do you -- do you recall how long it took you to conduct the investigations and prepare this particular report?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: It took about 140 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And did you -- did you complete that work alone?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: No, there was a whole team working on it. About five to six people, including me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And what was your position within that team?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: I set out the way to examine them, to examine the textiles. I was in charge of the whole investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please go to page 2 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, Ms. Maljaars, at the top of the screen we see the title "Materials Submitted," it indicates who it was received from. Via, we have J.R. Ruez. And date of receipt: 3rd of July, 1997. We then have some subheadings saying "originating from" and then a location. And below that a list of codes and some descriptions. Could you -- and that goes on for nine pages or so in the report. Could you tell us what those are, please?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: There are in total about 400 pieces of textile materials. They were divided from different origins, and the list on the page says the codes on the items and the origin that they came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And so these comprised the materials that you analysed in connection with this report?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And can we go to page 4 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Ms. Maljaars, did you have a correction that you wished to make?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I would like to point out a typo on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And could you tell us where that is, please?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: It's on the lower half. It's about the eight or nine line from below, and it says "LZ2-B-41 #2" and it should be "LZ2-B-41 #1."

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go to page 10, please. And if we focus on the bottom of the page it reads: "Question 1. "The ICTY requested to investigate the occurrence of similarities between the pieces of textile material, blindfolds, and ligatures from the different places of origin."

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Maljaars, here we see a series of subheadings, "Procedure," "Methods used" and "Exceptions," and that's all under the main heading of "Textile investigations - question 1." With respect to the heading "Procedure" in the second paragraph we read: "Within each group and from within each of the different origins within this group those pieces of textile material were selected that were the least deteriorated. Not all individual pieces of textile material in the different groups were therefore investigated." Could you please explain what this means?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: It means that we described all pieces of textile materials from all different origins, and we looked for similarities. When we found similarities between different origins, we looked for the best type of material that was the least deteriorated to investigate further.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you've mentioned material from different origins. What did you know about the origins of these pieces of material?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: I know they were different origins and with different codes and that there have been excavations revealing textile materials and that those materials were sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: All right. The next sentence reads: "... when working with the computerised database, it may be possible that there are more matches than those examined in the groups" I to IV. Could you explain what that means, please?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: We made a description of all the textiles that we received, and we did it on a special set of features. We put those features in database and then use the auto-filter to filter out the similarities or the similar description from different origins, and those five groups came out of that selection and it may be because of the way that we filtered the database that there are more matching pieces of textiles other than the groups I to V.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: All right. And the next subheading reads: "Methods Used." Now, we won't go through those because we don't have time, but were you familiar with and trained in the use of each of those methods?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: Yes, I was. When working for the NFI, I had two to three years training to do those investigations, as well as in my studies in laboratory school and in university I was trained to operate the FTIR machine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And were these methods consistent with the prevailing professional standards relevant to this sort of investigation at the time the report was prepared?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go to page 12, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: We see on this page "Results - question 1. "Group I." Very briefly, could you tell us what we're looking at here just in a couple of sentences?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: What we are seeing here is a table that I made stating all the features that are investigated, macroscopically and microscopically in FTIR, if applicable, and I used this table throughout the investigation of all textile materials, and it says how the features are on that specific type of textile material.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And is this group I of matching material one of a number of groups of matching material that you identified in your investigations?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: I am not sure I understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I see it says "Group I" here. Are there also additional groups that you identified in your report that contained matching textiles?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: Yes. Those were the groups II, III, IV, and V, as mentioned in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And I see at the bottom of the page there is a reference to FTIR-microscopy, and I see it says "not applied" and "not applied." Could you tell us what FTIR-microscopy was first, please?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: It's a method used based on spectroscopy to identify type of fibres, fibre types like polyester, nylon, acrylic, and you only apply them to synthetic fibres and not to natural fibres.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And so why was it not applied to fibres that comprised as group I?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: Because those contained cotton fibres.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go to page 27 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, Ms. Maljaars, could you tell us what we're looking at here, please?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: You're looking at a photocopy of two pieces of textiles from group I.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And are these photocopies of the textiles that you explained or that you had matched in the table that we just looked at?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And above the first piece of cloth, photocopy of the piece of cloth, is a code, and there appears to be another code below the second piece of cloth. What are those codes?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: The codes came with the pieces of textile.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So they are -- are they itemised in the list that we -- we looked at at the start of my questions?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please go to page 23 in the English, page 22 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Ms. Maljaars, we see at the top of the page it's "Conclusion - question 1," and focusing on group I, which is the group that we just looked at, can you briefly explain this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: When looking at the two pieces of textile, you immediately see similarities, and I conducted an investigation to see if those similarities are not there. So I took a number of investigations, investigated features, looked at the -- at everything that I could look at, and then I could see no differences between them; therefore, I stated that they are indistinguishable from each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you mentioned earlier that you had a team of persons working for you. Did you personally verify every match that you made in your report?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And in making that personal verification, did you in turn verify that with anybody else?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: Yes. All of my investigations were checked by another member of the textile and fibre group of the NFI.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go to page 43 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one additional question. You said it was verified by another member of the group. Were -- was that a person who had not participated in this investigation or was it someone who was within the team who was performing on this -- on this investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was someone who had already taken part in this investigation to describe the features of all the textile materials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So it was not an outsider to the group that worked on the investigation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Can we go to page 43 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Ms. Maljaars, here we see the title: "Figure illustrating the similarities between the pieces of textile with the different places of origin." Who prepared this table?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And does it contain the results of the textiles that you were able to match as represented by your report?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: It does as it -- as the arrows combine the different origins with each other. It does not combine the origins that are, for example, within the primary graves or within the secondary graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And what did you know about primary graves and secondary graves when you compiled this table?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: We found similarities -- no, we found the groups I to V, then we talked with Mr. Manning about what the results were, and I suggested we could make a figure illustrating how the connections could be made visible, and he made a separation in sites that were primary graves and sites that were secondary graves. And until that point, that was not known to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go to page 21 in the English and page 20 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Ms. Maljaars, could you explain briefly why you included this miscellaneous section in this report?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: The question originally was if we could see similar pieces of textile between all the origins. When we conducted that investigation, we came up with other features that may be important, so I put those features in this section.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And can you briefly describe those -- those features?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: The pieces of textile that we investigated from groups III, IV, and V, they were scalloped on one side, and in my report it says "eloped" on one side. So they did not match in a textile way but they did match in a way that they were found as in appearance, size, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And I see there is also a reference to groups IV and V.

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: Yes. The patterns that are woven in the textiles from groups IV and V are similar, and the colour of the textile is different but the weaving pattern is not different. It's the same. So we suggested they might have the same origin, like the same manufacturer or the same manufacturing process, and we thought that may be important to note beside then just answer the question that we were asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Lastly, let's go to page 10 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And focusing on the bottom of the page, there is a request. It states: "The ICTY also requested to investigate if it was possible to form a mechanical fit with textiles materials that are labeled," and then those labels are explained in that paragraph. Now, what were the results of that particular investigation?

utterances.speaker: SUZANNA MALJAARS
utterances.text: That a mechanical fit between those pieces was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender Ms. Maljaars' report, 65 ter 04612.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 04612 receives number P1771, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1771 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: That concludes my direct examination, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jeremy. I suggest, Mr. Lukic, that we'll not start for two or three minutes the cross-examination but rather start tomorrow. Therefore, Ms. Maljaars, we'll adjourn for the day and we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30 in this same courtroom. Meanwhile, I instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way about your testimony with whomever, whether that's testimony you've given today or whether that's testimony still to be given tomorrow. Is that instruction clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn for the day and will resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 16th of July, in this same courtroom III at 9.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 16th day of July, 2013, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.13 p.m.,
